Indian School of Business · Product Management · Case 40

Bakaya Labs: The Night Before the Board (A)

Discovery & Design → Problem & Opportunity Definition. A case for discussion. The company, its people and its figures are fictional; the market, the regulators and the named Indian firms around it are not.

1. Baner, Pune — Sunday, 11 October 2026, 11.40 p.m.

Revati Jadhav had printed the board pack twice, which was unlike her. The second copy was still warm and still wrong, in a way she could not yet put into a sentence a board would accept.

Outside, Navratri was in its first week and Dussehra nine days away; Diwali, and the quarter that brings Bakaya a third of its new business, was four weeks out. At nine the next morning Revati would take her seat as co-founder and chief product officer at the board meeting that would set the FY28 plan. Item four was a line she had written herself and now regretted: Product strategy — repositioning decision.

The facts were not in dispute. Annual recurring revenue stood at ₹33.20 crore at 30 September 2026, up from ₹30.10 crore at the FY26 close — 10.3 per cent in six months against 40.7 per cent for all of FY26. Net revenue retention on the April-to-September renewals was 82.9 per cent. Cash was ₹14.31 crore. And the module carrying the highest price on the order form, the analytics suite called Bakaya Bodh, was the one the renewal data said customers were quietly putting down.

What that meant was in dispute. Rishabh Joglekar, her co-founder and chief executive, had spent Saturday on a slide titled Bodh is why we win, and the win-loss data supported him. Rodrigo Jimenez in Toronto had spent it on a chart showing 108 of the 196 Bodh accounts unopened in September. Rupinder Jalota in Singapore had sent one line: the module isn't the problem, the customer is.

2. Company history, and the decision that is still in the room

Bakaya Labs was founded in Pune in March 2021 by Revati Jadhav, four years out of a product role at a Bengaluru payments company, and Rishabh Joglekar, a chartered accountant who had run indirect tax for an auto-component group in Chakan. The observation was narrow: every month, between the 14th and the 20th, every GST-registered company in India tries to make the portal's GSTR-2B statement agree with its own purchase register, and where they disagree, input tax credit is at risk.

Bakaya Reco matched the two line by line and listed the mismatches with the supplier GSTIN, the invoice number and the credit at stake. It sold for ₹1.8 lakh a year to firms with turnover between ₹100 crore and ₹1,000 crore. By March 2023 Bakaya had 142 customers and ₹3.4 crore of ARR, an average of ₹2.39 lakh each, on a ₹3.2 crore seed round; Bakaya Core was then bundled into every order form and the average contract rose to ₹7.19 lakh.

The decision that constrains Monday's agenda was taken in January 2025. Bakaya had closed a Series A of ₹38 crore in June 2024, led by Bhadrika Capital at ₹152 crore post-money — 11.9 times the ARR of ₹12.80 crore carried by 178 customers. The deck sold the view, not the matching engine: with purchase registers, GST filings, vendor masters and payment runs in one place, Bakaya would own the only clean picture of mid-market procurement spend in India, and the picture was the durable business.

So the Bengaluru team, under Rohan Jagtap, rebuilt the platform on a single shared semantic layer optimised for the aggregations analytics needs. Bodh was built on it; Reco was ported onto it. Twenty-one months later Reco runs against a store built for columnar aggregation rather than row-level joins, and for forty thousand purchase lines a reconciliation takes about eleven minutes against the ninety seconds Bharosa Compliance claims. Rohan's estimate for taking Reco off the shared layer is five to seven months of the Bengaluru and Pune teams' entire capacity, and ₹3.1 crore.

3. The industry

India's GST compliance software market is crowded at both ends and thin in the middle. At the base sits Tally, whose presence means almost every prospect already has a ledger it will not replace; above it, Zoho Books bundles compliance into a business operating system at a price that makes standalone modules look expensive. ClearTax has brand recognition in filing, IRIS Business Services and Cygnet are GST Suvidha Providers plumbed into the GSTN stack.

The regulatory cycle sets the rhythm: GSTR-1 by the 11th, GSTR-2B generated on the 14th, GSTR-3B and payment by the 20th. E-invoicing through the invoice registration portals has been extended down the turnover scale in phases, making the data cleaner and the matching job more tractable — a mixed blessing for a company whose first product was built on the mess. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 pushed consent and retention into contracts that two years ago did not mention them, with one consequence described below.

Bakaya's exposure abroad is small and disproportionately important. Of 338 customers, 14 are outside India, and one, Badar Metals Trading FZE in Jebel Ali, contributes ₹218 lakh of ARR — 6.6 per cent of the total and the largest contract the company has. Badar runs eleven legal entities across four Gulf jurisdictions and bought Bakaya in February 2025 almost entirely for consolidated reporting, which is to say for Bodh.

4. The situation in detail

The chronology matters: at each point the team believed something that has since turned out wrong.

April 2025. Bodh v2 was repriced from an included feature to a separate module at ₹6 lakh a year, with an attach target of 70 per cent on new logos; by September 2025 attach had reached 62 per cent and was celebrated at an all-hands. The belief: customers bought analytics because they valued analytics. The FY27 compensation plan pays a 1.5-times accelerator on any deal with Bodh attached.

January 2026. Bodh emails scheduled PDF packs to named recipients. In January, under the DPDP readiness programme, the tracking pixel and the per-recipient open log were removed; the decision took four minutes in a compliance review and nobody present worked on the product. Bodh now sends roughly 4,100 reports a month to 1,460 recipients across 171 of the 196 subscribing accounts, and nobody knows how many are opened.

April to June 2026. The FY24 three-year contracts and the first large FY26 annual cohort came up for renewal together. Downgrades began in the second week of April, consistently enough that Rupinder flagged it on 2 May. Rishabh's reading then, which he still holds, was a pricing problem in a bad quarter.

July 2026. Rodrigo circulated a four-page memo arguing that Bodh was a vitamin: valued in the abstract, bought in the demo, not used. Rohan's engineers, asked to confirm it, confirmed instead that the telemetry was incomplete. Both are true. The same month Bakaya Bachaav, a workspace for drafting replies to GST notices, went into pilot with 23 customers at ₹3.00 lakh a year — the most loved thing the company has shipped and the worst business, needing a chartered accountant in the loop at a delivery cost of ₹40.7 lakh against ₹69 lakh of ARR, a gross margin of 41.0 per cent against 82 per cent.

September 2026. Bharosa Compliance raised ₹120 crore and launched a standalone reconciliation product at ₹1.2 lakh a year — a little over a third of what Bakaya's Reco averages. On 30 September the half closed at ₹33.20 crore of ARR and 82.9 per cent net revenue retention. On 2 October Rukmini Jaisingh, group finance controller at Badar Metals, asked when the consolidation items promised in the February 2025 order form would ship.

5. The people

Revati Jadhav — co-founder and chief product officer, Pune
Holds that the company has measured the wrong thing and cannot price anything until it knows which jobs customers find urgent rather than useful. Owns 18 per cent. Not saying: the January 2025 architecture was as much hers as Rohan's, and the pivot means admitting the write-off.
Rishabh Joglekar — co-founder and chief executive, Mumbai and Pune
Holds that Bodh is why Bakaya wins and why it is worth ₹152 crore; the renewal problem is onboarding, not product. He leads the Series B conversation. Not saying: two prospective leads have told him informally that they price compliance tooling and analytics very differently.
Rohan Jagtap — vice-president, engineering, Bengaluru
Can deliver a fast standalone Reco or a year of Bodh improvements, not both; asked for both he will deliver neither. Three of his six senior engineers were hired for the semantic layer. Not saying: his five-to-seven-month estimate is a range because he has scoped the row-level join problem, not solved it.
Renata Jurek — head of design, Berlin
Holds that Bodh's usage measures a navigation failure, not an absence of need, and that her redesign — her only shipped initiative this year, at ₹47 lakh — fixes it. Not saying: six of her nine usability participants could not name a decision a Bodh dashboard would change.
Rodrigo Jimenez — staff data scientist, Toronto
Holds that the evidence Bodh is discretionary is strong enough to act on, and that waiting for better telemetry is a way of not deciding. The July memo is his reputation here. Not saying: Exhibit 5B was re-coded after a first pass disagreed too often, and that pass is unreported.
Rupinder Jalota — director, customer success, Singapore
Holds that the split is between kinds of customer, not modules: large accounts find the dashboards indispensable, small ones ornamental. Her expansion number depends on Bodh renewals. Not saying: she has told two large accounts the redesign arrives in January, which nobody has committed to.
Randall Jessup — senior vice-president, sales, Jersey City
Wants to lead with reconciliation, price it low and make dashboards an upsell; he believes he can double pipeline in two quarters on a painkiller story. His FY27 accelerator pays 1.5 times on Bodh attach, which he has not asked to change. Not saying: four of his six quota carriers missed in September.
Ramnath Julka — chief financial officer, Mumbai
Holds that there is no money for a transition; the plan must be funded from existing burn. He must present a fundable runway to Bhadrika Capital. Not saying: the 16.0-month runway in his board paper treats ₹83 lakh of costs as non-recurring, and the FY28 plan reinstates most of them from January 2027.

Two voices sit outside management. Roshan Jhingran of Bhadrika Capital, who led the Series A, chairs the product discussion and has twice said he will support "a sharper story, whichever story it is". Rukmini Jaisingh at Badar Metals holds a contractual right nobody at Bakaya has read aloud.

8. The options, as Revati currently frames them

Option 1: hold the bundle and fix adoption. Ship Renata's redesign, put customer success against the 108 Bodh accounts that recorded no session in September, and treat the renewal numbers as an onboarding failure. Cost: ₹1.6 crore over two quarters on top of the ₹47 lakh already spent. It preserves the Series B narrative, the Badar contract and the compensation plan, and fails if Bodh is genuinely discretionary for the 135 smaller subscribers.

Option 2: reposition around the acute problems. Lead with Reco and Bachaav, re-platform Reco for speed, price the entry point at ₹1.49 lakh to meet Bharosa, make Bodh a paid add-on. Cost: ₹3.1 crore and five to seven months of all engineering capacity. Ramnath's model assumes 60 per cent of Bodh ARR goes away — ₹658 lakh, or 19.8 per cent of current ARR — which none of the three cash readings in Exhibit 7 carries comfortably. It also opens the Badar termination-for-cause conversation and makes the lowest-margin product the headline product.

Option 3: run two products. Separate price lists, roadmaps and sales motions — compliance for the mid-market, analytics for the larger firms where Panel C says it sticks. Eleven hires and ₹2.4 crore annualised. Randall says his six quota carriers cannot run two motions, which may be a statement about his team or about the market.

Revati wrote these three on the whiteboard on Thursday and has been uneasy since, because each assumes the unit of decision is the module. Panel C says it might be the customer: of the 24 accounts above ₹500 crore of turnover, 21 kept Bodh, while of the 68 below, 32 dropped it and 13 left entirely. Exhibit 5 says something different again — that the most acute job, the notice reply at 31.0 hours an occurrence, arrives only 2.1 times a year and so costs 65.1 hours against the 78.0 hours the dull monthly reconciliation consumes, each over its own base. And Rupinder has twice raised a fourth possibility: that Reco belongs inside somebody else's distribution — a GST Suvidha Provider, or the channel of a ledger everybody already runs.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The board meets at nine on Monday 12 October 2026 and must approve the FY28 plan before the audit committee meets on 30 October. Cash is ₹14.31 crore at 30 September, with the three runway readings of Exhibit 7 and no agreement on which to plan against. The Badar Metals contract runs to 31 March 2028, is prepaid each April with ₹109 lakh unearned at 30 September, and carries a termination-for-cause right if the two Schedule 2 roadmap items slip past 31 March 2027. Rohan's capacity is one large programme a year, the FY27 compensation plan cannot be reopened without renegotiating six quota letters, and the ₹47 lakh Berlin retainer runs to 31 December 2026 and is non-cancellable.

The payback arithmetic the board will be shown mixes two bases, and Revati has marked it up twice. ₹9.82 lakh is average ARR across all 338 customers, while ₹14.2 lakh is the acquisition cost of the FY26 new-logo cohort alone; set against each other — 82 per cent gross margin on ₹9.82 lakh is ₹8.05 lakh of annual gross profit — they give a payback of 21.2 months, a figure about no actual cohort. The Reco-led comparison is worse: ₹4.14 lakh is the Core average over 338 customers and ₹3.14 lakh the Reco average over 241, so their sum of ₹7.28 lakh is not the average of any Core-plus-Reco order form but the sum of two differently based averages. On that number gross profit is ₹5.97 lakh and payback 28.5 months; Randall asserts acquisition cost would fall to ₹9.0 lakh, giving 18.1 months, and has no evidence for it. And Bharosa, ₹120 crore raised last month, will be in every one of those deals.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Using Exhibits 1, 2 and 3 only, say what problem each of Bakaya's four modules solves and whether the evidence that customers find it urgent is strong, weak or absent.
  2. Exhibits 2 and 4 point in opposite directions about Bodh. Which is the more reliable instrument, and what would you measure, and how, to settle it before Monday?
  3. Three downgrade rates follow from Exhibit 3, Panel B: 28 per cent, 43.6 per cent and 52.2 per cent. Which denominator is right for a pricing decision, and which for a board slide?
  4. Exhibit 6 ranks the arms in opposite orders depending on the metric. What should have been specified before the test, and what does arm B's ₹49,000 starter plan tell you about what was really tested?
  5. Exhibit 5 shows a job that is intense but infrequent, a job that is frequent but mild, and a willingness-to-pay figure that moves with the denominator. If Bakaya can fund only one job properly for eighteen months, which one, and what does that imply about price, buyer and sales motion?
  6. It is Monday morning, ten minutes before item four. What does Revati recommend, what is her one sentence to Roshan Jhingran about the customer, and what does she tell Rukmini Jaisingh that afternoon? Say which evidence here you are choosing to act against, and what you would need to see by March 2027 to know you were wrong.

At 12.20 a.m. the sound system below stopped and the silence was worse. Revati opened the renewal tracker and read the comment field on a lapsed account in Rajkot, a pipe maker with ₹340 crore of turnover and twenty-nine months of tenure: Not using the dashboards. Finance head says the matching is good but his consultant does the notices anyway. Asked for 40 per cent off, we offered 15, he went to nobody — he went back to Excel.

He went back to Excel. Revati read it twice. Somewhere in that sentence was either the case for Option 2 or the proof that none of the three options was about the right thing, and she could not tell which.

Vitamin or Painkiller? What Urgency Does to Adoption and Price

Ananya Deshmukh has eleven days to decide whether her burnout-alert feature is a nice-to-have her client can cut, or a cost-avoider her client cannot afford to lose — and the answer will set both the renewal conversation and the price.

A renewal eleven days out

Ananya Deshmukh, Vice President of Product at Rutuja Wellness Cloud, had eleven days before she sat across the table from Vikram Oberoi, head of human resources at Runjhun Technologies, a 6,200-employee IT services firm headquartered in Pune. The meeting was billed as a routine renewal conversation. In practice, it was a referendum on whether Rutuja's flagship wellness suite — guided meditation, sleep coaching, and financial-wellness nudges, priced at ₹42 lakh a year, or roughly ₹677 per employee — still belonged in Runjhun's budget for the year ahead.

The usage numbers Ananya had did not help her case on their own. Weekly active usage of the core suite sat at 18 percent, meaning that in any given week, five out of six Runjhun employees with access to a meditation app, a sleep tracker, and a savings nudge opened none of them. Vikram had said as much on their last call, not unkindly: “I believe in what you're building, Ananya. But my CFO is looking at every line that says ‘wellness’ and asking why we're paying for something eighty percent of people ignore.” Runjhun's attrition for the fiscal year just closed stood at 22 percent, against an industry rule of thumb that replacing a mid-level engineer — recruiting, onboarding, six months of below-full productivity — costs roughly 1.5 times annual cost-to-company, or about ₹14.25 lakh on Runjhun's average CTC of ₹9.5 lakh. Multiply that by the roughly 1,364 people Runjhun would need to replace that year, and attrition was costing the company upward of ₹194 crore annually. Against that figure, ₹42 lakh for a wellness suite was rounding error — but only if Vikram's board believed the suite was doing anything about attrition at all, and eighteen percent weekly usage was not evidence anyone could stand behind in a budget review.

That was the question Ananya needed to resolve before walking into that room: was Rutuja's product a vitamin — a thing people were glad existed, took occasionally, and would not lose much sleep over losing — or a painkiller — a thing whose absence someone would notice within a week and would pay to make go away? It was not an academic distinction. It would decide whether she defended a wellness perk or presented a retention tool, and those are different conversations in a different part of a CFO's budget, argued with different evidence and priced on a different logic entirely.

The idea: two shelves in the same medicine cabinet

The vitamin-versus-painkiller distinction sorts a product, or a single feature inside a larger product, by the answer to one question: if this thing disappeared tomorrow, would the person who relies on it go looking for a replacement today, or would they get around to it eventually — or never? A painkiller relieves a problem the person is already experiencing right now, one intense and specific enough that they will search for a fix unprompted, pay before they are fully convinced, and forgive a clumsy product because the alternative is worse. A vitamin improves something the person is not currently suffering over; it is valuable the way a balanced diet is valuable — true in aggregate, over years, and easy to skip on any given Tuesday without visible consequence.

The metaphor has no single credited inventor, and that is itself informative: it survives because it names something pharmacy retail and pharmaceutical sales teams had already noticed for decades. A shelf of prophylactic supplements moves slowly and depends on marketing, packaging, and habit; the same store's stock of paracetamol and antacids moves the moment someone's head or stomach hurts, with almost no persuasion required. Technology and venture circles borrowed the language explicitly during the industry's boom years of the mid-to-late 2000s, when early-stage investors evaluating hundreds of pitches a month needed a fast heuristic for separating “this is delightful but optional” from “someone would bleed money without this.” The framing stuck because it answers a question every product leader eventually has to face under pressure: not is this valuable — almost anything a competent team ships is valuable to someone — but is it valuable enough, to someone in enough pain, that they act now rather than later?

The single sentence Ananya could say in Vikram's office without sounding glib was this: urgency, not usefulness, is what makes someone pay before they are convinced. It has the merit of being falsifiable. She could test it against Rutuja's own data instead of asserting it and hoping it landed.

How the sort actually works

Working out where a product sits is not one judgment call; it is a short sequence of questions applied in order, and the order matters because a later step can overturn what an earlier one seemed to establish.

The first question is who feels the problem, and how often — not who benefits, since nearly every stakeholder can be shown a benefit on a slide, but who experiences the problem's absence as a felt, personal cost, and on what cadence. For Rutuja's meditation and sleep modules, the honest answer was: the individual employee, occasionally, when a bad night or a stressful week made the app briefly relevant, and never in a way that stopped them from doing their job the next morning. For Early Warning — the module whose fate Ananya was really deciding — the honest answer was different. The problem was felt not primarily by the employee, who mostly did not know the module existed (it ran quietly on calendar density, after-hours login timing, and a two-question fortnightly check-in), but by Vikram's HR business partners, and one level up by Vikram himself, every time a resignation letter arrived from someone his team had not seen coming.

The second question is to quantify the cost of inaction in the unit the buyer already keeps score in, not the unit the vendor prefers. Ananya's mistake in an earlier pitch to a different client had been to talk about “reduced stress scores.” Vikram did not budget in stress scores; he budgeted in attrition percentage and cost-per-hire. Reframed that way, the same underlying signal — this employee's workload and sleep pattern look unsustainable — became a number the CFO's office already tracked every quarter, which made it arguable rather than merely plausible.

The third question, and the one practitioners most often skip because it demands evidence rather than a good story, is whether people already go looking for a fix without being asked. Ananya could point to her account team's log: no Runjhun employee had ever raised a ticket asking where the meditation module was, but three separate HR business partners had, unprompted, asked in the two quarters before Early Warning existed whether the platform could flag “people who look like they're about to burn out.” Unprompted demand that arrives before the product does is close to the cleanest evidence a painkiller can offer.

The fourth question is to test whether that willingness to act survives contact with price and effort, not just intention. A manager telling an interviewer “yes, that would be useful” is cheap; a manager reallocating a direct report's workload, or a CFO approving a new budget line, is expensive — and only the second counts as evidence. Ananya's pilot, walked through below, supplied exactly this harder kind of proof.

The fifth question, the one most frameworks leave out entirely, is whether the classification is stable or contingent on a trigger. Products migrate shelves over their life. The sort has to be re-run whenever the surrounding context changes materially — a regulation passes, a competitor has a public failure, a downturn squeezes discretionary budgets — rather than treated as a label fixed at launch.

The arithmetic of an early warning

Between October 2025 and February 2026, Ananya's team ran Early Warning as a quiet pilot inside Runjhun, scoring risk from calendar load, after-hours login frequency, and the fortnightly check-in, with no employee-facing dashboard — only a private alert routed to that person's manager. Of Runjhun's 6,200 employees, 400 were flagged as high risk at some point in the window. Of those 400, managers acted on 340, rebalancing a project, approving deferred leave, or simply having a direct conversation; the remaining 60 went unaddressed, mostly because the manager was between roles or the alert was missed in a busy sprint.

The comparison Ananya needed was straightforward, if the numbers were laid out rather than described. Company-wide attrition for the year was 22 percent. Among the 340 flagged employees whose managers intervened, attrition came in at 9 percent. Among the 60 flagged but not acted upon, it was 27 percent — slightly worse than the company baseline, consistent with the idea that a flagged risk left untouched is at least as dangerous as no signal at all. The gap that mattered was the 13-percentage-point difference between the intervened group and the company baseline: 340 employees × 13 percent = 44.2 departures avoided, each worth roughly ₹14.25 lakh in avoided replacement cost, for a total of just over ₹6.3 crore in a single fiscal year. Rutuja's ask for the Early Warning add-on was ₹18 lakh a year. Set against ₹6.3 crore in avoided cost, that is a return on the module's price of roughly 35 times — the kind of ratio that survives even generous skepticism about how much of the gap was really caused by the intervention rather than by manager quality alone.

Eight nuances a learner must sit with

1. The quadrant depends on whose seat you are sitting in.

The single most common error is plotting a product on the frequency-intensity grid from one vantage point and forgetting that a different stakeholder occupies a different point entirely. From the employee's chair, Early Warning is felt rarely, if at all — most employees never trigger it. From Vikram's chair, a version of this problem crosses his desk every week, in the form of a flagged case, a resignation, or a question from the CFO. Painkiller status is not a property of the problem in the abstract; it is a property of the problem as experienced by whoever holds the wallet or the pain, and those can be two different people.

2. Rare does not mean unimportant — it can mean insurance.

A problem that is felt rarely but catastrophically when it strikes — a server outage, a compliance breach, a single resignation of an irreplaceable architect — behaves like insurance rather than a daily painkiller, and insurance is still bought with real urgency once the buyer has been burned once. Learners who plot only on frequency and ignore intensity will misclassify a low-frequency, high-severity product as a vitamin, when it is closer to fire-extinguisher economics: nobody uses it most weeks, and everybody wants it in the building.

3. A vitamin can still be indispensable.

Being a vitamin describes the shape of demand — low urgency, dependent on habit and marketing — not the size or importance of the value delivered. Toothpaste is a vitamin by this definition: nobody wakes up in acute pain over its absence, yet nearly everyone uses it daily and would notice its disappearance within a week. The framework predicts how hard a company will have to work to get someone to adopt and keep paying, not whether the underlying benefit is trivial.

4. Painkillers get vitaminized by competition and time.

Consumer basic antivirus software was a painkiller in the 1990s, when a virus could destroy a home computer's only copy of a family's photographs; it is close to a vitamin today, bundled invisibly into operating systems, because the acute fear that once drove urgent purchase has been engineered away by the market itself. A classification made this year is not a classification for all years; the diagnostic in step five of the sorting sequence exists precisely because painkillers decay.

5. The buyer's urgency and the user's urgency can point in opposite directions.

In a B2B2C structure like Rutuja's, Vikram experiences Early Warning as urgent while most Runjhun employees experience it as invisible or mildly reassuring at best. This split is not a flaw to be argued away; it has to be designed around. Selling on the buyer's painkiller urgency while quietly building the habits that make the user side sustainable — rather than assuming buyer urgency alone guarantees usage — is the actual job, and confusing the two audiences is how modules get bought once and never renewed.

6. Willingness to pay is not the same test as painkiller status.

A government-run mental health helpline addresses an intensely painful, urgent problem and is free at the point of use; a person in crisis who calls it is unmistakably experiencing painkiller-level need, yet no transaction occurs. Absence of payment tells you about the buyer's budget and the market's structure, not about whether the underlying pain is real. Conflating “nobody pays for this” with “this is a vitamin” leads teams to abandon genuinely urgent problems simply because the economics of the specific market have not yet been solved.

7. The framework says nothing about product quality or defensibility.

A well-built vitamin can outlast a poorly distributed painkiller, because adoption pull is only one input into a business's survival; distribution, trust, and switching cost matter independently. Painkiller status buys a company an easier first sale, not a permanent moat — a lesson closely tied to nuance four, since a painkiller that fails to build any of those other advantages before the market catches up simply gets commoditized on schedule.

8. The honest diagnostic questions are behavioral, not attitudinal.

A thoughtful newcomer should resist asking “would you find this useful” and instead ask three sharper questions: what does this person do today, without our product, when the problem occurs? What would they have to give up or reprioritize to act on our alert this week rather than next quarter? And would they have paid for this, or gone looking for it, before we showed it to them at all? Answers built from observed behavior — support tickets, workaround spend, unprompted requests — are far harder to talk yourself into than answers built from a nodding head in an interview room.

Consumer, B2B, marketplace — and early-stage versus scale

The shape of this distinction changes with who is buying and who is using, and Ananya had two other cases in her own portfolio that made the contrast concrete. Rutba Fit, a standalone consumer meditation and habit app Rutuja had considered acquiring the year before, sold directly to individuals with no employer or HR layer standing between the product and the wallet. There, the vitamin problem is at its purest and most stubborn: no economic buyer exists to feel urgency on the user's behalf, so the entire burden of creating enough habit and perceived stakes to survive January's resolution-driven signups and February's cancellations falls on product design and marketing alone. Consumer vitamin products live or die on retention curves, not on a single persuasive pitch to a budget-holder.

Ruvaan Freight Exchange, a two-sided logistics marketplace matching truck owners with shippers that Ananya had advised informally, illustrated a third pattern: the two sides of a marketplace can sit in entirely different quadrants simultaneously. A truck owner with an empty vehicle experiences every idle day as direct, intense cash loss — a textbook painkiller, checked compulsively, several times a day. A shipper choosing how to move a consignment typically already has a trusted broker relationship and experiences the marketplace as a mild, occasional convenience — closer to a vitamin, opened when the usual broker is unavailable. A marketplace has to identify which side is more painkiller-driven and bootstrap liquidity from that side first, because trying to court the vitamin side before the painkiller side is solved usually stalls the whole exchange; Ruvaan's early growth came almost entirely from truck-owner urgency, with shipper habit built only afterward, once enough trucks were reliably available to make the marketplace worth a shipper's occasional look.

Scale changes the calculation again. An early-stage company almost always needs a painkiller to acquire its first paying customers, because it has no brand trust to lean on and cannot yet win purely on habit or bundling; urgency does the persuading that reputation would otherwise do. A large, established company can sustain genuinely vitamin-shaped products for years, because the marginal cost of offering one more module inside an existing relationship is close to zero, and because switching an entire vendor relationship over one unused feature is rarely worth a customer's effort. This is precisely Rutuja's structural tension: the core suite survives as a vitamin bundled inside a broader HR relationship, while any genuinely new line of revenue, like Early Warning, has to justify itself on painkiller terms because it is being sold, and priced, on its own.

Each of these mistakes shares a root cause: substituting a story that feels true for a measurement that could prove it false. The fix in every case is the same discipline Ananya applied to Early Warning — find the behavioral trace the claim would leave if it were true, and go look for it before committing a price or a pitch to the claim.

What good looks like

A useful contrast came from a smaller Rutuja client, a 900-employee logistics firm, where the HR head had built a habit of tying wellness spend directly to a regulatory hook rather than to sentiment. When the Ministry of Labour and Employment's occupational safety and health code began drawing attention to employer duties around psychosocial risk, and against the backdrop of obligations already established under the Mental Healthcare Act, 2017, that HR head reframed the entire wellness suite — including its quieter, vitamin-shaped modules — as part of a documented duty-of-care programme rather than a discretionary perk. The reframing did not change the product; it changed what would happen if the client did nothing, converting a soft, deferrable want into a defensible, auditable obligation. Renewal at that account happened in nine minutes, not because usage numbers had improved, but because the cost of inaction had become concrete, external, and time-bound. That is the general shape of a well-handled decision: not forcing every module to pretend to be a painkiller, but finding or building the real trigger, structural or regulatory, that makes inaction visibly expensive to the person who signs the cheque.

What Ananya decides

Ananya walked into Vikram's office and did not defend the meditation suite as a retention driver, because the data did not support that claim and pretending otherwise would have cost her credibility on the one number that did hold up. Instead she split the pitch in two. The core suite stayed priced and described as what it was: a modest, bundled wellness benefit worth keeping for the same reason a canteen subsidy is worth keeping, not because it moves attrition, but because removing it would generate a different, smaller kind of resentment. Early Warning was priced separately, at ₹18 lakh, presented with Table 1's numbers exactly as measured, and pitched explicitly as a retention-cost-avoidance tool aimed at Vikram's own KPI rather than at general wellbeing. She also told him, honestly, that the module's return depended on his managers actually acting on the alerts, and offered a manager-training add-on to protect that assumption — turning the Tier-2 scenario's lesson into a safeguard rather than a caveat buried in a footnote.

Vikram approved both lines within the week. What convinced him was not the size of the number but its shape: a painkiller argument, built from behavior his own team had already exhibited, priced against a cost his own CFO already tracked.

The next thing worth learning, for anyone who has followed this argument to its end, is how frequency and intensity translate into a defensible price once a product's quadrant is settled — because knowing that something is a painkiller only tells you people will act; it does not yet tell you how much they will pay, or how that number should move as the pain itself evolves. Two questions are worth sitting with in the meantime: what would have to change in your own product for a feature you currently treat as a vitamin to become, for at least one class of user, genuinely urgent? And whose seat are you standing in when you answer that question — the person who feels the problem, or the person who signs for the fix?

Vitamin, Painkiller, or Obligation

Two product leaders, nine weeks apart, discover that the vitamin–painkiller question they thought they were answering about their products is really a question about their buyers' decision environments — and that the most valuable shelf in the pharmacy is neither the analgesics nor the supplements.

Assumes the working treatment of this topic: the frequency–intensity grid, the five-question sort, whose-seat-are-you-in, and the fact that painkillers decay. This page starts where that one stopped.

1. Two decisions, nine weeks apart

On the morning of 9 March 2026, Nandita Rao sat in a meeting room above the shop floor at Jantar Instruments' Chakan facility with a single slide on the screen and a board that wanted an answer by lunch. Jantar made wireless vibration and thermal monitoring nodes for rotating industrial assets — pumps, compressors, gearboxes, motors — and sold a diagnostic layer on top of them that predicted bearing failures, misalignment and lubrication faults some weeks before the asset stopped. The company had closed the financial year with ₹24 crore of revenue across 214 live plants, most of them auto-component suppliers and food processors in Maharashtra, Tamil Nadu and Gujarat. A typical installation covered 40 critical assets: ₹18,000 per node in hardware, or ₹7.2 lakh in year one, plus ₹6,000 per asset per year for the software, or ₹2.4 lakh of recurring revenue. The hardware was profitable enough. The software was the business.

The slide showed two uses for ₹6.4 crore of growth capital. The first was to take the field sales organisation from twenty-two people to forty-four, on the theory that Jantar's problem was coverage: India had several thousand plants that fit the profile and Jantar was in front of perhaps six hundred of them a year. The second was stranger, and Nandita had written it herself. It proposed spending the same money building a joint programme with Jaanib General Insurance, a mid-sized general insurer whose equipment-breakdown book covered a large slice of exactly the plants Jantar wanted. Under the programme, a plant that kept its critical assets continuously monitored on Jantar's platform would receive a credit against its machinery-breakdown premium. No new features. No new sensors. Only a change in who else had an opinion about whether the plant bought.

Girish Apte, Jantar's chief executive, had put the objection plainly in the pre-read. “We have spent four years learning that predictive maintenance is a painkiller,” he wrote. “When a compressor seizes and a line stops, we sell in six weeks. The answer is more people in more plants finding more pain, not a scheme that hands our customer relationship to an underwriter.” He was not wrong about the six weeks. Nandita had the numbers that proved it, and they were the reason she had stopped believing his conclusion.

Nine weeks later, on 22 April 2026, Shreya Kamat faced the mirror image of Nandita's problem in a very different building. Jaanch Legal AI occupied one floor of a converted bungalow in Bengaluru's Richmond Town and sold an AI drafting and review copilot to in-house legal and compliance teams at mid-market Indian companies. On every metric a product leader is taught to admire, Jaanch was outstanding. It had 118 paying accounts and 4,900 seats at ₹1,100 per seat per month, or ₹6.47 crore of annual recurring revenue. Seventy-one per cent of seats were active in any given week. The median active user opened it 4.2 times a week. Net promoter score was 62. Support tickets were overwhelmingly requests for more, not complaints about less.

And yet net revenue retention was 97 per cent and falling; seat expansion had run at four per cent over the previous year; the realised price per seat had drifted from ₹1,450 eighteen months earlier to ₹1,100; two competitors were at ₹390 and a third had begun bundling a comparable capability at no incremental charge. Sixty-one per cent of Jaanch's competitive losses were not to competitors at all but to no decision. Shreya's co-founder, Aftab Qureshi, summarised the board's mood in one line: “We have built something people use every day and nobody has to buy.”

Put the two companies side by side and the standard treatment of vitamins and painkillers starts to creak. Jantar sells into visible, expensive, physically obvious pain and cannot get the plant to act. Jaanch sells into a problem so mild that nobody would call it pain, and gets 71 per cent weekly engagement. One product is used rarely and hurts badly when absent; the other is used constantly and would barely be missed. Both have a demand problem, and it is the same demand problem wearing two disguises. The argument of this page is that the vitamin–painkiller binary is not a claim about a product, or even about a problem. It is a cheap, usually serviceable prior on a measurable quantity — the rate at which a particular buying unit converts a latent need into a purchase decision without being pushed — and that once you write that quantity down, it decomposes into five factors, only one of which most teams ever work on. The factor with the highest leverage, and the one with the longest half-life, is not pain at all. It is obligation.

2. The idea, stated precisely, and the schools that disagree about it

Begin with the definition the working treatment gives and then sharpen it until it can be measured. A painkiller relieves a problem the buyer is experiencing now, intensely enough that they will seek a remedy unprompted. A vitamin improves a state the buyer is not currently suffering over. The sharpening move is to notice that “will seek a remedy unprompted” is a rate, not a state. For any defined buying unit — one plant, one legal department, one household — there is some probability per month that it initiates a purchase process for a given class of remedy without a vendor prompting it. Call this the initiation hazard, written as the Greek lambda. A painkiller is a product class for which lambda is high enough that demand arrives as pull; a vitamin is one for which lambda is low enough that all demand must be pushed. There is no boundary, only a continuum and a threshold set by the economics of your go-to-market: if your fully loaded cost of creating one qualified conversation from cold is ₹40,000, then the hazard that separates a company that grows on inbound from one that grows on outbound is wherever ₹40,000 becomes unaffordable.

The metaphor's origin is retail pharmacy, and the working treatment is right that no single person is credited with importing it into technology. But the idea has at least four respectable intellectual ancestors, and knowing them is what lets you referee an argument between two competent practitioners who are each using a different one without saying so.

The first and most formal is Noriaki Kano's model of quality, developed in Japan in the late 1970s and published in 1984, which sorted product attributes into must-be qualities whose absence causes dissatisfaction but whose presence causes none, one-dimensional qualities where satisfaction scales with performance, and attractive qualities that delight when present and are not missed when absent. Kano's must-be and attractive categories map almost exactly onto painkiller and vitamin, with two advantages the later metaphor lost: Kano was talking about attributes within a product rather than whole products, and he supplied a survey instrument with a functional and a dysfunctional question for each attribute, which forced the analyst to ask what happens if this is absent rather than merely whether it is liked.

The second is prospect theory, Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky's 1979 account of decision under risk, which supplies the mechanism the metaphor lacks. Losses loom larger than equivalent gains. A painkiller is a product whose value is naturally framed as a loss avoided; a vitamin's value is naturally framed as a gain obtained. The same rupee of economic value therefore moves a budget at different speeds depending only on the frame, which is both the most useful and the most ethically loaded fact in this entire topic, and we will come back to it.

The third is Clayton Christensen's jobs-to-be-done tradition, which rejects the binary as a category error. In its developed form — the four forces of push, pull, anxiety and habit — urgency is not a property to be classified but a resultant of four vectors that can be worked on independently. A JTBD practitioner will tell you, correctly, that vitamin and painkiller collapse four measurable forces into one label, and that the collapse is exactly where the misclassifications come from.

The fourth is the enterprise-sales qualification tradition, which since the MEDDIC framework developed at PTC in the early 1990s has treated the compelling event — a dated, external consequence of not deciding — as a field to be filled in on every opportunity. That tradition's distinctive and uncomfortable claim is that the compelling event is usually constructed in conversation rather than discovered, which makes urgency an output of the selling process and not an input to the product decision.

These lineages produce genuinely different schools, and the productive way to distinguish them is to ask what proposition each would sign.

The obligation school deserves a moment of attention because it is the least discussed and, on the evidence, the most commercially consequential. Take the pharmacy metaphor seriously for once and ask which shelf actually generates the profits. It is not the analgesics. Paracetamol is a commodity sold in strips for a few rupees, bought under acute need, by a buyer who will accept any brand and forget the purchase within a day. The pharmaceutical industry's most valuable franchises have historically been chronic maintenance therapies — statins are the canonical case — taken daily, for decades, by people who feel absolutely nothing before or after taking them. By the naive metaphor, a statin is a vitamin: no felt pain, no acute need, a benefit that is real only in aggregate and over years. It is nevertheless one of the largest categories in the history of medicine. The reason is that a third party stands between the patient's indifference and the purchase: a physician operating under a clinical guideline, reimbursed by an insurer, audited against outcomes. The patient does not need to feel urgency, because the system supplies it on a calendar.

That inversion is the spine of this page. Felt pain and third-party obligation are two independent axes, not one. The classical frequency–intensity grid lives entirely on the first axis. Adding the second produces four cells with materially different economics.

3. Mechanics in depth: decomposing the hazard

An expert does not classify a product; an expert decomposes a hazard. Nandita's working model, which she had built over three quarters out of Jantar's own CRM and installed-base data, treated the monthly probability that a plant initiates a purchase conversation on its own as the product of five terms. Each term is independently observable, which is the point of the exercise; the value of the model is not its predictive accuracy, which is modest, but that it makes it impossible to assert urgency without saying which term you are claiming.

The first term, frequency (f), is the number of times per month the buying unit experiences an instance of the problem. This is the term teams measure best and over-weight most. For a Jantar plant, unplanned stoppages of a critical asset ran at 1.6 per month. For a Jaanch legal team, drafting or review tasks that the copilot could shorten ran at 22 a month. Jaanch's frequency is fourteen times Jantar's, which is why its engagement is so much higher — and which explains nothing at all about its price.

The second term, relative intensity (i), is where most models go wrong. It is not the absolute cost of one occurrence. It is that cost expressed as a fraction of the buyer's notice threshold: the amount below which a cost is absorbed into ordinary operating noise without anybody escalating it. Every buying unit has one, and it is usually discoverable by asking the finance business partner what size of variance triggers a written explanation. At Jantar's typical plant the median unplanned stoppage cost ₹2.4 lakh in lost output and overtime, against a notice threshold of about ₹5 lakh, giving i = 0.48. At Jaanch's legal teams a single drafting task consumed perhaps three hours of a lawyer's time, worth roughly ₹1,900 fully loaded, against a notice threshold of ₹1.5 lakh, giving i = 0.013. This single number is the whole of Jaanch's commercial predicament. The problem occurs constantly and is genuinely annoying, and every individual instance of it is more than a hundred times too small for the organisation to notice. Frequency without intensity produces engagement, affection and no pricing power, which is precisely the configuration Shreya was staring at.

The third term, attributability (a), is the probability that the buyer can trace the cost to this problem rather than to noise. This is the silent term. At Jantar's plants, root cause was formally logged for about a third of stoppages; the rest were recorded as “machine trouble” and absorbed into a general sense that the plant was badly run, so a = 0.35. At Jaanch, attributability was near-perfect at 0.9, because a lawyer knows exactly how long a contract took. Note the inversion again: the product with the trivial problem has excellent attribution, and the product with the expensive problem cannot prove where the money went. Attribution is also the term most amenable to being solved by the product itself, which is why so many successful industrial and compliance products begin life as measurement tools that the customer buys in order to discover how much the problem was costing.

The fourth term, substitute sufficiency (s), is the share of the pain already relieved by whatever the buyer does today. It enters the model as (1 − s), and it is the term that determines your price ceiling, because you are paid for the increment over the workaround, not for the value of the problem. Jantar's plants mostly bought quarterly route-based vibration surveys from an external agency — a technician with a handheld meter, walking the plant four times a year — which caught a meaningful fraction of developing faults, so s = 0.55. Jaanch's users had general-purpose AI assistants on their laptops that did perhaps seventy per cent of the drafting job for nothing, so s = 0.70.

The fifth term, budget accessibility (b), is the probability that the person who feels the problem can reach money within the quarter. Jantar's plant head had perhaps ₹3 lakh of genuine discretion; a ₹9.6 lakh first-year commitment required corporate capital approval through a window that opened once a year, so b = 0.25. Jaanch's head of legal could approve ₹1,100 a seat on an existing software line without asking anyone, so b = 0.60.

The five terms multiply, scaled by a fitted constant that absorbs everything the model leaves out. Nandita calibrated the constant on one segment where she had clean data — Jantar's inbound enquiry rate ran at 6.2 per cent of the installed-base-adjacent population per year, or 0.52 per cent a month — which gave k = 0.17. She then held k fixed and varied the terms to ask what the two available strategies would do.

Figure 2. The same five-term chain applied to four scenarios. Jantar's baseline self-initiation of 6.1 per cent a year rises to 42 per cent without a single change to the sensor or the algorithm, purely by raising attributability (the insurer's loss data does the attribution the plant cannot do for itself) and budget accessibility (the spend is netted against a premium that is being renewed regardless). Jaanch's copilot, despite fourteen times the event frequency, sits at 9.1 per cent because its intensity term is 0.013.

Three things about this model matter more than its arithmetic. First, the terms are not equally elastic. Frequency is a property of the world and you cannot change it. Intensity you can sometimes change by re-aggregating — twenty-two sub-threshold events a month become one supra-threshold event a quarter if you can get the buyer to look at them as a pool, which is exactly what a dashboard, a scorecard or a register does, and is why so much enterprise software is in the business of summing small pains into a visible one. Attributability you can almost always change, because measurement is cheap. Substitute sufficiency changes underneath you, especially in AI-adjacent categories, and you should assume it is rising. Budget accessibility is the term teams treat as fixed and is in fact the most movable of all, because it depends on which budget line you present to, and that is a choice.

Second, the model is multiplicative, which means any term near zero kills the product regardless of how strong the others are. This is the formal statement of a thing experienced practitioners know in their bones: a product with an enormous, obvious, expensive problem and no reachable budget is dead, and so is a product with a perfect budget path and a problem below the notice threshold. You cannot compensate.

Third, and the reason Nandita presented it to the board with an explicit caveat: the fitted constant absorbs the model's ignorance, the independence assumption is certainly false, and if you calibrate on one segment and extrapolate to a very different one, the constant will be wrong. It is a bookkeeping device for forcing honesty about where an urgency claim comes from. It is not an instrument. An expert uses it the way a good analyst uses a discounted cash flow: for the discipline of the assumptions, not the precision of the answer.

4. When the frame applies, and when it actively misleads

State the conditions as testable claims and apply each to both protagonists.

Claim one: the frame applies when there is a single buying unit that both feels the problem and controls the money. Where feeling and paying separate, the binary begins to mislead, because the product is simultaneously a painkiller for one party and a vitamin for another. At Jantar this holds partially: the maintenance head feels every stoppage and controls almost nothing; the plant head controls ₹3 lakh; the group capex committee controls the rest and feels nothing. Jantar is therefore not a painkiller in any useful sense at the point where the decision is actually made. At Jaanch the buying unit is coherent — the head of legal both suffers the drafting load and signs for the tool — which is precisely why Jaanch has excellent adoption and no pricing power: a coherent buying unit with a sub-threshold problem simply buys a cheap thing and is happy.

Claim two: the frame applies when the problem's cost per instance exceeds the buyer's notice threshold, or can be credibly aggregated until it does. Jantar passes at i = 0.48 per instance and would pass overwhelmingly on an annual aggregate of ₹46 lakh of unplanned downtime. Jaanch fails per instance by two orders of magnitude and passes only in aggregate — 22 tasks a month across eight lawyers is roughly ₹40 lakh a year of professional time — but aggregation is a rhetorical act that the buyer has to accept, and heads of legal are not paid on hours saved, so the aggregation lands as a slide rather than as a budget.

Claim three: the frame applies when the substitute is clearly inadequate. Both protagonists fail this. Jantar competes against quarterly manual surveys that work about half as well for a fifth of the price. Jaanch competes against a general-purpose model that costs the customer nothing incremental. In both cases the price ceiling is set by the increment, and in both cases the sales narrative has been built around the total value of the problem, which is why both companies discount.

Claim four: the frame is actively misleading whenever the purchase is on someone else's calendar. This is the condition the classical treatment misses entirely. Statutory filings, audit cycles, insurance renewals, accreditation reassessments, plant shutdowns, and the annual capex window are all dates that arrive whether or not anybody hurts. A product that can attach itself to an existing date inherits that date's urgency without needing any of its own. Asking “is this a painkiller?” of such a product produces a false negative every time. Nandita's whole proposal is an attempt to attach Jantar to the insurance renewal, which happens on a fixed date, requires no capex approval, and involves a counterparty whose actuarial tables do the attribution Jantar's customers cannot do for themselves.

Claim five: the frame is misleading when the product is sold into a budget line whose evidence standard it cannot meet. The same product sold on five different lines behaves like five different products. 5. Hard edge cases

Multi-product portfolios, and the load-bearing vitamin

In a portfolio, classification has to be done at the level of the module and the decision at the level of the system, and the two answers frequently conflict. Jaanch's copilot is a discretionary vitamin by every measure in section 3. The obligation register Shreya wanted to build depends, for its completeness, on the copilot: the register is only trustworthy if every contract and every filing obligation in the company has passed through a system that reads them, and the copilot is the reason documents pass through Jaanch at all. Kill the vitamin on the grounds that it does not pay for itself and the painkiller's data goes stale within two quarters. The formal way to see this is that the copilot's contribution is not its own revenue but the attributability term of the register — it moves a from perhaps 0.4 to 0.75 — and no portfolio review conducted on revenue per module will ever show that. Mature companies handle this badly and in a characteristic way: the rationalisation exercise is run by finance on a revenue-per-product basis, the loss-making module is cut, and the consequences appear eighteen months later in the renewal cohort of a different product, attributed to competition.

Two-sided structures, where the pain and the money sit on different sides

Jaldoot Water Systems, a Pune company Nandita knew through a shared investor, sold inline water-quality sensors and a reporting layer into two kinds of customer. On one side were large residential complexes, where the resident welfare association felt the problem weekly — discoloured supply, complaints, a tanker called at short notice — and bought in eleven weeks for ₹1.4 lakh a year with an eighty-eight per cent renewal rate. On the other were municipal bodies and water utilities, where the engineer felt nothing at all but had statutory reporting obligations, and who bought through tender in fourteen months for ₹47 lakh with essentially no price flexibility. Jaldoot's temptation, every year, was to abandon the small side. The reason not to was that the residential contracts generated the continuous sensor data that made the municipal reporting credible, and the residential complaints generated the political pressure that put water quality on the municipal agenda in the first place. The general pattern: in two-sided structures, felt pain buys you speed and price, obligation buys you size and predictability, and the two sides are usually coupled by information. A marketplace or platform strategy that optimises the sides independently will break the coupling and then wonder why the obligated side's willingness to pay collapsed.

Hardware plus software

Jantar's own seam is the classic one. The node is a capital item bought once, installed by an electrician, bolted to a gearbox, and forgotten. The software is a recurring subscription whose value accrues only if somebody logs in. Jantar's software renewal rate was 94 per cent at year two and 71 per cent at year three, and the drop had nothing to do with product quality. What happened at year three was that the maintenance engineer who had championed the installation moved on, the hardware kept working, the dashboard stopped being opened, and the renewal arrived on the desk of a finance manager who could see a recurring charge and could not see a user. Physical installation creates the illusion of stickiness while destroying the visibility that recurring revenue depends on. The counter-practice, which Jantar had only partly adopted, is to push a small quantity of unavoidable, dated output into somebody's inbox — a monthly asset-health certificate that the plant head signs — so that the software has a calendar presence independent of anyone's curiosity. Note what that is: a manufactured, mild obligation, invented by the vendor because the market did not supply one.

Regulated markets, where obligation is exogenous and revocable

The obligation cell in Figure 1 has the best economics and one catastrophic failure mode: you do not control the mandate. Section 8's failed case is exactly this. The discipline that experienced practitioners in regulated categories apply is to distinguish one-off mandates — a single implementation date, after which the demand pulse passes — from rolling obligations such as annual audit, triennial accreditation, quarterly filing or insurance renewal, which recur forever and cannot be complied with once. Companies that build on one-off mandates have a boom and a cliff. Companies that build on rolling obligations have annuities. The two look identical in a pipeline report and are distinguished by one question: after the first compliance event, what forces the customer to do this again?

AI-native products, where the substitute term is non-stationary

Every term in the hazard model is assumed stable over a planning horizon except, at present, substitute sufficiency. Jaanch's s was 0.45 when the company launched in 2023 and 0.70 by early 2026, and nothing Jaanch did caused the change; the general-purpose models simply got better at the specific job Jaanch had built a company around. A product whose intensity term is small survives only on the size of (1 − s), and if s is rising at ten points a year, the product has a computable expiry date. This is the structural reason so many AI-native application companies with superb engagement metrics have weak pricing: they occupy the frequent-and-mild cell, where the only defence is a substitute gap, and the substitute gap is the one thing improving on someone else's roadmap. The compensating gift AI gives is on the other side: it collapses the cost of attribution. Reading every contract in an enterprise and extracting every dated obligation was, before 2023, a consulting engagement costing more than the risk it quantified. When measurement becomes nearly free, obligation plays that were previously uneconomic become buildable, which is why the same technology that is destroying Jaanch's copilot is what makes Jaanch's register possible.

The organisational seam

Inside the company, the classification is rarely held by one function, and the disagreement is structural rather than personal. Sales is rewarded on closed business this quarter and therefore has every incentive to describe the product as a painkiller; the compelling-event field in the CRM will be filled in, one way or another. Product owns retention data and knows the thing is used twice a month. Pricing usually sits with finance and is set from a value model that neither of the other two believes. Customer success inherits the gap between the pitch and the product and has no authority over either. The observable symptom of an unresolved seam is a widening spread between the urgency implied by first-year marketing and the urgency demonstrated by second-year usage, and it is paid for in month-thirteen churn by whoever is running customer success at the time. Mature companies say they resolve this with a positioning document. What they actually do, in the good cases, is maintain a shared library of compelling events with observed win rates attached — so that the claim “this is urgent” becomes a testable statement about a named trigger rather than a mood — and they audit the library against outcomes once a year.

6. Ten distinctions that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

One: high engagement is evidence about habit, not about urgency, and the two are routinely confused because they are measured with the same instrument. The tell-tale sign is the combination Shreya was looking at: weekly active share rising, net promoter score high, realised price falling. A competent practitioner reads that as a monetisation problem to be fixed with packaging. The expert reads it as a statement that the value being delivered is denominated in a currency the organisation does not count — usually individual time — and that no packaging change can convert a currency the buyer does not bank. The obvious reading is wrong because engagement measures how pleasant it is to use the product given that you have it, and urgency measures what happens if you do not, and there is no reason those should correlate.

Two: urgency is a stock that drains on a measurable schedule, not a state a customer is in. The tell-tale sign is a correlation between discount depth and elapsed time since the customer's triggering event, which almost every B2B company has in its CRM and almost none has looked for. The obvious reading is that the rep discounted badly or the deal went stale. The expert reading is that the deal did not go stale; the organisation healed, and the eighty-five-day half-life is a property of the customer's institutional memory rather than of the sales process. Once you believe that, response latency becomes a first-class product and go-to-market metric, and territory-based coverage models start to look indefensible.

Three: the classification describes the buying unit's decision environment, not the problem. The tell-tale sign is two customers with identical problems, identical size and identical industry taking eight weeks and eleven months respectively. When you investigate, the difference is never about the severity of the pain; it is about who could reach money and whether anyone could prove the cost. The obvious reading — that the slow customer is less mature or less pained — is wrong and is the reason so much pipeline is disqualified for the wrong reason. The right disqualification question is not “how badly does this hurt?” but “who here can spend, and what would they have to show?”

Four: attributability is the silent multiplier, and customers who cannot attribute will agree with you and never buy. The tell-tale sign is a prospect who enthusiastically confirms the problem is severe and, asked what it cost them last quarter, cannot say. Competent practitioners treat this as a need for education and send a case study. Experts treat it as a product opportunity: sell the measurement first, cheap or free, let the customer discover their own number, and return with a remedy priced against a figure the customer generated. The obvious reading is wrong because the missing thing is not belief, it is evidence the buyer can put in front of someone else.

Five: a substitute that half-works is worse for you than no substitute at all. The tell-tale sign is the sentence “we manage it in a spreadsheet and it's fine.” Competent practitioners hear that as validation — look, they already do this manually, the need is proven. Experts hear a price ceiling. You will be paid for the increment over the spreadsheet, which is a fraction of the problem's value, and the spreadsheet has the decisive advantage of already being approved. This is why categories with no incumbent workaround at all, where the customer currently does nothing, sometimes support higher prices than categories full of manual effort, which is the exact opposite of the intuition most discovery training instils.

Six: obligation outlasts pain, and the durable franchises are things nobody feels. The tell-tale sign is the answer to a single question — who audits this? — and an expert asks it in the first discovery call. The obvious reading is that painkillers are the premium category because urgency commands price. They do command price, once, briefly, and then the organisation heals on an eighty-five-day half-life. An obligation does not heal; it returns next quarter with a date on it. The strategic implication, which sounds cynical and is not, is that the highest-leverage product work in many categories is not making the pain worse or the relief better but finding the party — regulator, auditor, insurer, accreditor, customer's customer — who already has authority to make inaction costly, and making it trivially easy for that party to exercise it.

Seven: manufactured urgency is a loan taken out against a renewal eighteen months away, and the person who takes it is never the person who repays it. The tell-tale sign is not a month-three churn spike but a month-thirteen one, concentrated in accounts sold by the most successful reps. The obvious reading blames onboarding or the customer-success team. The expert reading is that the compelling event asserted at the point of sale was real enough to close and not real enough to survive measurement, and that the gap has been sitting on the balance sheet, unrecorded, for a year. The honest boundary — and this is a boundary of judgement, not of technique — is that framing an existing consequence more vividly is legitimate and often a service to a buyer who had not connected two facts; asserting a consequence whose magnitude you have not estimated and could not defend is not.

Eight: painkiller positioning invites measurement, and vitamins are never audited. The tell-tale sign is the customer proposing a quarterly business review with outcome metrics on it. Competent practitioners celebrate the engagement. Experts recognise that they have just accepted an attribution burden, and immediately ask whether they would survive an honest measurement of it. This is the least intuitive nuance on this list, because it means there are situations where the correct decision is to decline to position as a painkiller despite being able to win the deal that way — where the value is real but not cleanly separable from confounders, and a rigorous customer will one day run the control group.

Nine: trigger concentration is a portfolio risk that looks exactly like product-market fit. The tell-tale sign is simple and countable: the distribution of answers in the “why now” field of the CRM. When more than about a third of weighted pipeline gives the same answer and that answer is a date somebody else controls, the company has a correlated exposure that no sales forecast will show, because forecasts model each deal's probability independently. The obvious reading is momentum in a category. The expert reading is a single point of failure with a pipeline attached.

Ten: value-based pricing gives you a ceiling; the hazard tells you how much of the ceiling you can actually collect and how long collection takes. The tell-tale sign is the familiar and demoralising gap between a value model that says the product is worth ₹40 lakh a year to the customer and a market that pays ₹6 lakh. Competent practitioners conclude the value model is wrong or the sales team is weak. Usually neither is true: the value is real, and the fraction of it you capture is governed by attributability, substitute sufficiency and budget accessibility, not by the size of the value. Raising captured price therefore almost never comes from a better value narrative and almost always comes from moving one of those three terms — instrumenting attribution, widening the gap to the substitute, or changing which budget line you present to.

7. How this differs by product type and company stage

In consumer markets, the buying unit is coherent and the notice threshold is low, which makes the classical frame at its most reliable and its most brutal: with no economic buyer to feel urgency on the user's behalf and no auditor to supply obligation, a consumer vitamin lives entirely on habit formation and distribution. The obligation axis is not absent — insurance requirements, school mandates, employer subsidies, statutory road-safety equipment and doctor's instructions all create consumer obligation — but it is rarer and mostly outside the product team's reach. The honest position for a consumer vitamin is not to pretend to be a painkiller but to accept that the fight is over retention curves and channel economics and to staff accordingly.

In B2B mid-market, which is where both protagonists sit, the decisive variable is budget accessibility, because the gap between what a function head can approve unilaterally and what requires a committee is enormous and sharply bounded. A great deal of apparent urgency variation between accounts is really variation in this threshold. Pricing to sit just under the unilateral-approval line is a real and underused strategy, and it is why so many products cluster at suspiciously similar per-seat prices.

In enterprise, the frame's usefulness inverts: urgency is so thoroughly a product of the buying process — the compelling event, the mutual action plan, the fiscal-year boundary — that classifying the underlying product tells you little. What matters is whether the seller can locate an existing dated consequence. Enterprise is where the obligation cell dominates most completely, and where the largest software franchises in history have been built on things nobody enjoys.

In platforms and marketplaces, the standard advice is to bootstrap from the side with more urgency, which is right as far as it goes. The refinement the Jaldoot case supplies is that the urgent side and the paying side are often different sides, and that the urgent side's value to the business may be informational rather than financial. Deciding which side to serve on revenue alone will, with some regularity, cause you to cut the side that makes the other side's product work.

In hardware and physical goods, the painkiller is very often not the good but a service wrapped around it. Jamdani Looms, a handloom apparel brand selling ₹9,000 to ₹22,000 garments direct to consumers, ran two adjacent offers. A fabric-care subscription — detergents, storage bags, seasonal reminders — was a textbook discretionary vitamin: 6 per cent attach, 41 per cent annual renewal, and the first thing cancelled. A re-weave and repair service was a painkiller: only 4 per cent of customers used it in a year, but a snagged thread on a ₹14,000 garment is an acute, dated, emotionally loaded problem, and 62 per cent of repair users bought again within six months against a 31 per cent base rate. The lesson generalises: in physical goods the object is usually the vitamin and the failure of the object is the painkiller, so the service layer is where urgency and loyalty both live.

In AI-native products, everything said in section 5 applies, with one addition about stage. An AI product's engagement metrics mature far faster than its pricing power, because the technology makes the first ten minutes delightful and does nothing about the notice threshold. Teams therefore reach a false milestone — excellent usage, enthusiastic users, strong qualitative feedback — six to twelve months before they discover they have no pricing power, and by then they have hired against the wrong signal.

By stage: a company before product-market fit needs pull, and therefore needs either felt urgency or an obligation it can attach to, because it has neither brand nor distribution to substitute. A growth-stage company's characteristic error is the opposite — it has proven it can sell a painkiller during triggering events and then attempts to scale by covering more territory, when the arithmetic in Figure 3 says it should be reducing latency to triggers instead. A mature company can carry genuine vitamins indefinitely, because the marginal cost of one more module inside an existing relationship is near zero and no customer changes vendors over an unused feature; its characteristic error is believing that the vitamins are surviving on merit, and discovering otherwise during the first serious procurement review.

8. Three worked cases, one of them a failure

Case A: Jantar and the three-party arithmetic

Nandita's insurer proposal only works if it is positive for three balance sheets at once, and the discipline of writing all three down is what separated it from a partnership slide. Take the representative plant: 40 critical assets, an insured machinery value of roughly ₹40 crore, an equipment-breakdown premium at 0.38 per cent, or ₹15.2 lakh a year.

Figure 4. The monitoring software costs the plant ₹2.4 lakh and returns ₹2.74 lakh of premium credit, so the recurring decision is free at the point of purchase before any downtime benefit is counted. The evidence base under the 57 per cent figure is the part Nandita expected to be attacked, and she presented it without softening. Across 8,900 asset-years of monitored operation, Jantar had recorded 41 catastrophic failures against an expected 96 at the unmonitored baseline failure rate of 1.08 per cent per asset-year — 55 failures avoided, at an average claim of ₹31 lakh, or about ₹17 crore of avoided loss set against ₹5.34 crore of software revenue on those same assets.
