The unadjusted arithmetic that vendors in her category habitually present — taking the full downtime cost of every avoided failure, assuming the monitoring caused all of it, ignoring that plants which install monitoring are systematically better-run plants — would have produced a number above twenty. Her point to the board was that an unadjusted twenty is worthless to an underwriter and a defensible 3.2 is bankable, and that the entire strategy depended on being able to survive an actuary's scrutiny. This is nuance eight in operation: the moment Jantar claims to be a painkiller in a form an insurer will price, it has accepted an audit, and the audit is the asset.

Case B: Jaanch and the three routes out of the affection trap

Shreya's team spent six weeks in the customer base before modelling anything. They read 2,600 live contracts across the 118 accounts and found 312 with notice or renegotiation windows falling in the next twelve months, and 47 that had already auto-renewed unnoticed in the preceding year at an average value of ₹19 lakh. Assuming, conservatively, that 40 per cent of those would have been renegotiated and that renegotiation typically recovers 11 per cent, the hard, defensible saving across the whole base came to roughly ₹39 lakh a year, or about ₹33,000 per account. This was, she told the board, the single most important number in the analysis, and it was disappointing: the honest, measurable cash value of the painkiller was less than a third of what the accounts already paid for the vitamin. Any strategy built on claiming penalty avoidance or hard savings would collapse the first time a customer measured it.

Case C: Jatan Care Cloud, and what a failure of this reasoning costs

In 2024 the company made what looked like the smartest possible version of the obligation play. An enforcement notification tightening documentation requirements for clinical establishments was expected in the state where most of its pipeline sat, and Jatan built its entire year around it. By September 2024 it had 84 qualified opportunities, a weighted pipeline of ₹19 crore against a plan of ₹11.4 crore, a sales team scaled from nine to twenty-six, and a monthly burn of ₹62 lakh.

In November 2024 the notification was deferred by eighteen months. Pipeline conversion, forecast at 38 per cent, came in at 7 per cent. Revenue for the year was ₹3.1 crore against the ₹11.4 crore plan. Runway fell from fourteen months to five; the company cut from 61 people to 34 in February 2025 and raised a bridge at terms the founders described in their investor update as instructive.

The early warning had been visible for at least two quarters and nobody had looked for it, because there was no reason to look at a pipeline that was growing. Of the 84 opportunities, 71 had the same entry in the “why now” field. Eighty-five per cent of weighted pipeline rested on one date controlled by a third party. The diagnostic question that would have caught it takes nine words — if this date moves by a year, which deals survive? — and the honest answer in September 2024 was thirteen of eighty-four. Jatan's failure was not that it bet on a regulation; regulatory tailwinds are legitimate and often decisive. It was that it bet on a one-off mandate and staffed as though it had an annuity, and that it never separated the deals that would exist anyway from the deals that existed only because of the date.

The recovery took fourteen months and is worth reading closely because it was not a pivot. Jatan kept the product. It changed four things. It re-anchored to rolling rather than one-off obligations, principally hospital accreditation cycles, which recur on a multi-year clock with a pre-assessment phase roughly six months ahead and which the hospital initiates itself. It repriced from a ₹14 lakh annual licence to a ₹2.4 lakh base plus per-event and per-bed charges, which halved the approval height and let the product enter on the compliance line rather than the capital line. It added an insurance-claims-denial module — denied claims are felt weekly, in cash, by a revenue-cycle manager who can attribute them precisely — as a genuine painkiller wedge whose function was to get Jatan into the hospital at all. And it imposed a rule that no single external trigger could account for more than 30 per cent of weighted pipeline, enforced by the head of sales at the weekly forecast meeting.

The second is that the cost column escalates with the distance between the person who creates the exposure and the person who discovers it. 10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Three of these disagreements are live enough that competent, well-informed practitioners take opposite sides in the same room, and none of them is resolved by the evidence currently available.

Whether manufactured urgency is legitimate practice or a transfer from the future. The strongest version of the case for manufacturing runs like this: buyers are not rational calculators with complete information about their own losses; most organisations genuinely do not know what a problem is costing them; and a seller who assembles that evidence and presents it vividly is performing an analytical service the buyer could not perform for itself. The 3.2-to-one ratio Nandita computed was not visible to a single one of her customers before she computed it. On this view, refusing to frame consequence is not neutrality but a failure to inform. The strongest version of the case against is that framing and fabricating lie on a continuum with no natural boundary, that the incentives all point one way, and that the cost of over-framing lands eighteen months later on a different team. What would settle it is cohort evidence: if accounts sold with a strong consequence frame retain at month 24 as well as accounts that arrived with their own urgency, the objection dissolves. Most companies have this data and almost none have run the comparison, because the comparison is professionally uncomfortable for whoever commissions it.

Whether obligation-seeking is product strategy or rent-seeking. The obligation school's case is straightforward and empirically strong: the most durable software categories on earth — accounting, tax, payroll, audit, safety, regulatory filing — are ones where a third party requires the work, and building for those categories is not manipulation but recognising where society has decided the work must happen. The counter-case has two parts. The first is prudential: mandates are exogenous, revocable and politically contingent, as Jatan discovered, so a strategy resting on one is resting on someone else's decision. The second is ethical, and sharper: a company whose growth depends on obligations expanding has an interest in obligations expanding, and the distance between advocating for a standard your product satisfies and lobbying for a standard only your product satisfies is shorter than anyone is comfortable admitting. Serious practitioners land in different places on this and the difference is a difference of values, not of analysis.

Whether the binary should survive at all. The jobs-to-be-done position is that a two-label classification of a five-term phenomenon is worse than useless because it is confident, and that practitioners given the four forces make better calls than practitioners given two shelves. The defence of the binary is not that it is accurate but that it is fast, memorable and available in the moments when classification actually happens — the second minute of a customer conversation, the third slide of a pitch, the corridor after a board meeting — and that a heuristic which is right seventy per cent of the time and gets used beats a framework that is right ninety per cent of the time and gets used at offsites. What would settle it is a straightforward experiment nobody has run properly: give matched groups of practitioners the same discovery transcripts under time pressure with different frameworks and compare their classifications against what the accounts actually did. Until somebody does, this is a genuine open question, and both camps are arguing from selected recollection.

Two smaller disagreements are worth naming. Consumer practitioners largely hold that urgency is a sales artefact and that retention curves are the only durable signal; enterprise practitioners largely hold that retention without a compelling event is just inertia waiting for a procurement review. They are both generalising correctly from their own markets and incorrectly to each other's. And there is an unresolved argument about whether the frame survives at all in AI-native categories, where substitute sufficiency moves faster than a planning cycle; the honest answer is that nobody has enough years of data yet to say whether that instability is a transitional feature of a young technology or a permanent condition of the category.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this topic classifies products. Someone who has internalised it does seven or eight things differently, and they are all observable.

They ask “which budget line?” before they ask “is this urgent?”, because they know the first question determines the discount, the cycle, the evidence standard and the renewal test, and the second is largely downstream of it. They date their classifications and put the re-check in a calendar, because they have seen a painkiller decay into a vitamin over four years of competitive parity and know it happens without an announcement. They instrument attribution long before they need it, often shipping measurement as the first version of the product, because they know attributability is the term that silently destroys deals with customers who agree with everything they say. They price against the increment over the workaround rather than the value of the problem, and they are not embarrassed by the smaller number. They keep a written library of compelling events with observed win rates and they audit it, which means their sales organisation's urgency claims are falsifiable statements rather than moods. They watch the concentration of their own triggers as carefully as a lender watches sector exposure. They can state, without looking it up, the number their customer's finance function already tracks, in the units that function uses, because they know an argument denominated in the buyer's own metric is worth more than an argument that is merely true.

And the most distinctive tell: they are comfortable saying out loud that a product of theirs is a vitamin and that they intend to win it on distribution, habit and bundling rather than on urgency. The competent practitioner under pressure reaches for a painkiller story because painkiller stories fund roadmaps. The expert knows that a vitamin honestly described can be built into a durable business and that a vitamin dressed as a painkiller cannot, because the costume has to be maintained at every renewal by people who were not in the room when it was designed.

12. What each of them decided

Nandita split the ₹6.4 crore rather than choosing, but not down the middle and not as a compromise. ₹4.1 crore went to the Jaanib programme, structured as a two-region, forty-plant, twelve-month pilot with three conditions she insisted on in the term sheet: Jantar retained the right to sell direct into any account; the distribution fee was capped at 15 per cent and the exclusivity window at eighteen months, to limit channel capture; and the programme carried an explicit reversal trigger — if the loss ratio on monitored assets did not beat the unmonitored book by at least 35 per cent over the pilot, Jantar would exit rather than renegotiate. The remaining ₹2.3 crore went to the field organisation, but not as territory coverage. It funded an incident-response desk with a service standard of a quote within fourteen days of any reported stoppage at any plant in the addressable base, monitored or not, which is the operational expression of Figure 3's eighty-five-day half-life. Nandita also declined something: a proposal to reposition the platform around energy efficiency, which polled well with plant heads and which she rejected on the grounds that motor energy savings are real but confounded by load, season and tariff, so the attributability term would collapse under exactly the scrutiny the insurance route was designed to invite.

Girish accepted it with one recorded dissent, which the board minuted: he believed the insurer would, within three years, either build the capability or squeeze Jantar's margin to the point where the channel was worth less than the direct business it displaced. Nandita's answer was that he was probably right about the three years and that the eighteen-month exclusivity cap was her acknowledgement of it.

Shreya chose Route C, with two commitments that were not in the spreadsheet. The copilot's price would not be raised, ever, because its function in the system was adherence and corpus freshness rather than revenue, and raising its price would cost seats, and seats were what made the register trustworthy. And Jaanch would not market penalty avoidance. The claim it would make was narrower and auditable — that the obligation register was complete, current and exportable in a form an auditor could sign against — because the ₹33,000 per account of hard savings would not survive a customer's own measurement, and section 6's eighth nuance says that a painkiller claim you cannot defend under audit is worse than the vitamin claim you could have made honestly. She set a falsifier with a date: if register attach was below 35 per cent of accounts by January 2027 and the pull ratio was still under 0.3, the reposition was wrong, and Jaanch would return to being a cheap, beloved tool and fight on distribution without pretending otherwise.

Discussion questions.

  1. Nandita's insurance route raises Jantar's self-initiation rate roughly sevenfold without changing the product, but it hands attribution, and eventually pricing power, to a counterparty who can build the capability itself. Girish's dissent may be right. Under what conditions should a company decline a demand mechanism it does not control, even when the arithmetic in Figure 2 is this favourable?
  2. Shreya refused to market penalty avoidance despite believing the penalty exposure is real, on the grounds that she could not defend the number under audit. Is that the correct standard for a product claim, or is it an unusually strict one that will cost her the market to a competitor who is less careful? What would change your answer?
  3. Jatan's recovery cost 41 per cent of average contract value and nine points of gross margin. If you had been in the room in September 2024, with a pipeline growing and a plan being beaten, what would you have had to believe to argue for capping single-trigger concentration at 30 per cent — and who in the organisation has both the information and the standing to make that argument?

13. Going deeper

Frequency and intensity of the problem
The two terms this page decomposed further. Worth returning to with the notice-threshold idea in hand, because the standard treatment measures intensity absolutely and the useful measure is always relative to what the buying unit escalates over.
Writing a problem hypothesis
A hypothesis that names the buying unit, the event frequency and the budget line is testable in a fortnight; one that names a persona and a pain is not. This is where the five terms become sentences someone can go and check.
Surfacing assumptions
Every term in Figure 2 is an assumption wearing a decimal point. The discipline of listing them separately is what stops a single confident estimate of “urgency” from hiding four unexamined beliefs inside itself.
Riskiest assumption first
In a multiplicative model the riskiest assumption is the term closest to zero, not the one you are least sure about. For Jaanch it was intensity at 0.013; for Jantar, budget accessibility at 0.25. This gives the prioritisation rule a quantitative basis.
Validating a problem hypothesis
Unlocks the behavioural evidence standards that separate a nodding head from a reallocated budget — unprompted search, workaround spend, and the pull ratio used in Table 4 as the empirical proxy for the hazard.
Persevere, pivot or perish
Jatan's fourteen months are a worked instance. The distinction that matters there is between a wrong problem, which requires a pivot, and a right problem reached through the wrong trigger, which requires a repricing and a new door.
Opportunity solution trees
Where the classification stops being a judgement and becomes a structure: each of the five terms is a branch with its own candidate solutions, which is how “make it more urgent” decomposes into work a team can actually schedule.

Jantar Instruments, Jaanch Legal AI, Jatan Care Cloud, Jaanib General Insurance, Jamdani Looms and Jaldoot Water Systems are fictional composites constructed for teaching purposes; their figures are illustrative and internally consistent rather than drawn from any single firm.

Ashvik Rokad: Vitamin or Painkiller

A decision case on problem urgency, adoption and pricing

1. Opening

On the morning of Monday, 12 October 2026, Pallavi Iyengar, chief product officer of Ashvik Rokad, sat in a glass meeting room on the fourth floor of the company's Baner office in Pune with a single sheet of paper in front of her. It held three lines, each a possible use of the company's next engineering quarter. By Friday, 16 October, the roadmap had to be frozen, because the board would meet the following week and Diwali in early November would pull half the team away from their desks.

Ashvik had spent three years building a mobile bookkeeping app for small shopkeepers. It was well liked and widely installed. Yet only three in every hundred monthly users paid for anything, and the company had roughly fourteen months of cash left. The chief executive, Pradeep Idris, had asked Pallavi a plain question: which of the three ideas would shopkeepers go out of their way to buy, and which would they admire and then forget?

2. Company background

Ashvik Rokad was founded in 2019 by two former Infosys engineers who had watched their parents' general store in Nashik run on a school notebook. The app replaced that notebook. A shopkeeper records credit sales, sends a reminder to customers through WhatsApp, and sees a running balance. It competes directly with Khatabook and OkCredit in the digital khata space, with Vyapar in small-business billing, and, at the upper edge, with Zoho Books and Tally, which serve merchants who already employ an accountant.

At the start of October 2026 Ashvik had 6,20,000 registered merchants, of whom 1,86,000 opened the app at least once a month, or 30 per cent. Of those monthly actives, 5,580 paid for Rokad Plus, a subscription at ₹99 a month that adds backups and printable statements; that is 3.0 per cent of the monthly actives. Rokad Plus therefore brings in about ₹5.52 lakh a month, or ₹66.29 lakh a year. The company raised ₹38 crore in a Series A round in 2023 and had ₹26.6 crore in the bank on 1 October, against a monthly burn of ₹1.9 crore. That gives the fourteen months of runway Pradeep had in mind.

The payment landscape also matters. Because UPI, run by NPCI, now carries most small retail payments in India, a shopkeeper can collect money instantly, and the old difficulty of "I have no change" has largely disappeared. What remains is the problem of customers who buy on credit and pay late. Any collections feature that Ashvik builds would use Razorpay as its payment aggregator, which means Ashvik would not expect to need its own RBI authorisation to hold customer funds, although it would confirm this with counsel before launch.

3. The situation

In the summer, Pallavi's team had interviewed sixty shopkeepers and small traders in Pune, Nashik, Indore and Coimbatore. They asked about three kinds of trouble that the product might address, and about whether the person would pay roughly ₹200 a month, or its annual equivalent, for relief. 4. The people

Pallavi herself had joined from a large e-commerce firm and distrusted features that sounded impressive in a board deck. Pradeep Idris, the chief executive, wanted a plan that would lift paid conversion from 3 per cent to a figure investors would call healthy, and he wanted it before the next fundraise. He leaned towards the dashboards because they were cheapest and because Zoho and Tally had made "insights" respectable in the market.

Pranay Inamdar wanted a low-risk quarter for a team that had been stretched by a platform migration, and he would carry the burden of any partnership with Razorpay or with chartered accountants. Petra Ilgner wanted the product to feel calm, and thought that a reminder feature which nagged customers might embarrass shopkeepers in small towns where everyone knows everyone. Pushkar Ivatury wanted an experiment before a commitment. Poornima Ishwar wanted, above all, relief for the merchants who phoned her, since she was the one who heard their stories first.

6. Questions for discussion

  1. Using Exhibit 1, classify each of the three problems as a painkiller or a vitamin. Which two features of the data drive your classification, and where do they disagree?
  2. Pushkar noted that 27 merchants said they would buy GST help while only 18 had received a notice. What does that gap suggest about stated willingness to pay, and how should it change the conversion rates assumed in Exhibit 3?
  3. Option A recovers its cost fastest, yet Option C is the stronger business by the end of the year. Reconcile these two statements using the revenue-per-year, build-cost, months-to-recover and still-paying-after-12-months columns of Exhibit 3.
  4. If you were Pallavi, what would you present on Friday, what would you ask Pradeep to accept as the evidence bar, and what would you tell Poornima and Petra?

7. A note for the learner

This case turns on a single test: is the problem one that people seek out a remedy for, or one they would only accept if it were offered free? A painkiller is frequent, intense and recognised by the sufferer, and it is bought at the moment of pain. A vitamin is a good thing that nobody feels the lack of on a given morning, so it is bought rarely, kept briefly and priced low. Exhibit 2 makes the distinction visible. Dashboards sit at the bottom of the chart, widely wanted but barely felt. Late payments sit in the top right, both common and sharp. The GST notice sits at the top left, intense but infrequent.

Frequency and intensity also set price and adoption. A frequent painkiller supports a monthly subscription and builds a habit, which is why option C retains 78 per cent of buyers. An infrequent painkiller sells like insurance, in an annual lump, and is at risk of being forgotten until the day it is needed. A vitamin is a feature to include in an existing plan, not a product to charge for separately.

One defensible path is to build Option C, but to stage it. Before committing the full ₹110 lakh, release a paywalled pilot of the reminder-and-link flow to a tenth of the monthly actives, or 18,600 merchants, and measure actual payment instead of stated willingness. Pushkar's caution is right, and Exhibit 3's 6.0 per cent conversion is an assumption that a pilot can test. If the pilot shows paying at well under that rate, the 5.0-month recovery stretches accordingly, and the board should hear this before the vote, not after. Meanwhile, ship a basic version of the dashboards inside the existing Rokad Plus tier as a retention aid, since their weak intensity argues against a separate price. Option B should wait: its demand is real but seasonal, and it will be easier to sell once Ashvik has a daily habit in the app and a base of merchants who trust it with their money.

A reasoned answer should also name what would change the decision. If the pilot's conversion fell near 2 per cent, or if shopkeepers reported damaged relations with customers, Option B or a slimmer Option A would deserve another look. The student's task is not to find the single correct number but to show that the choice follows from the pain observed in the market and not from the ease of the build.
